policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: The readings differ only in whether ἐν stands before the dative φωνῇ, and ASV 'he cried with a mighty voice' renders the plain dative and ἐν with the dative alike as 'with'.
ASV 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great' repeats the verb, so the doubled ἔπεσεν ἔπεσεν is the text it rendered and not the single-verb reading.
δαιμονίων and δαιμόνων are alternative genitive plurals of the same word, and ASV 'a habitation of demons' is identical under either.

ASV gives only two φυλακή clauses — 'a hold of every unclean spirit, and a hold of every unclean and hateful bird', each carrying the note 'Or, prison' — so the added clause 'and a hold of every unclean beast' was not in its text.

ASV 'all the nations are fallen', with its note 'Some authorities read of the wine . . . have drunk', excludes πέπωκαν but cannot distinguish πέπτωκαν from πέπτωκασιν, which are the same perfect rendered 'are fallen'.
The variant is the number of the imperative, plural Ἐξέλθατε against singular Ἔξελθε, and English 'Come forth' is the same for both.

The readings differ in the position of ἐξ αὐτῆς relative to ὁ λαός μου (and, between the first two, only in punctuation), and ASV 'Come forth, my people, out of her' cannot report a Greek order that its own syntax fixes.
ASV prints 'unto her' in italics in 'and double unto her the double', marking it as a supply, so the added αὐτῇ was not in the text it rendered.
The variant is the article τὰ before διπλᾶ alone, and English 'the double' requires an article whether or not the Greek has one.
ASV 'the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her' is present tense, so κλαίουσιν καὶ πενθοῦσιν rather than the future κλαύσουσιν καὶ πενθήσουσιν is the text it rendered.
Accusative αὐτήν and dative αὐτῇ after the verbs of mourning are both rendered 'over her', and ASV marks no difference of case.
ASV 'and pearls' is plural, so μαργαριτῶν rather than the singular μαργαρίτου is the text it rendered.
πορφύρας and πορφυροῦ are noun and adjective for the same commodity, both rendered 'purple' in ASV's list.
ASV has 'and spice' with the note 'Greek amomum', which renders καὶ ἄμωμον, so the reading that omits the phrase is not the text behind this list.
ASV 'and cattle and sheep' keeps the order κτήνη καὶ πρόβατα, and a coordinated list of nouns carries its order into English, so RP's πρόβατα καὶ κτήνη is not the text it rendered.
The readings differ in where σου stands and whether τῆς ἐπιθυμίας is present in the string, and ASV 'which thy soul lusted after' places the possessive where English requires it.
ASV 'and men shall find them no more at all' renders οὐκέτι by 'no more' alongside οὐ μή 'at all', so the reading that omits οὐκέτι is not the text it rendered.
ASV 'and men shall find them no more at all', with 'men' italicized as a supply for an impersonal third plural, renders εὑρήσουσιν and not RP's second-singular εὕρῃς.

ASV runs 'weeping and mourning, saying, Woe, woe' without a conjunction before the participle, and it renders καί as 'and' throughout this chapter, so the reading with καὶ λέγοντες is not the text it rendered.
The variant is the presence of ἐν before the dative of material, and ASV 'decked with gold' renders the bare dative and ἐν with the dative alike as 'with'.
ASV 'and precious stone and pearl' is singular, so μαργαρίτῃ rather than the plural μαργαρίταις is the text it rendered.
Aorist ἔκραξαν and imperfect ἔκραζον both fall together in ASV's simple past 'and cried out as they looked upon the smoke'.
Aorist ἔκραξαν and imperfect ἔκραζον both fall together in ASV's simple past 'and cried, weeping and mourning'.
ASV 'weeping and mourning, saying, Woe, woe' has no conjunction before 'saying', so the reading that adds καί after πενθοῦντες is not the text it rendered.
μύλινον and μύλον are adjective and noun for the same object, and ASV 'a stone as it were a great millstone' renders either the same way.
Singular αἷμα and plural αἵματα are both rendered 'the blood of prophets and of saints', English having no usable plural of 'blood'.
